title: Spatial partitioning
sub: "Who is within range" without O(n²): a uniform grid and a spatial hash, rings for k nearest, quadtrees and BVHs, OverlapSphereNonAlloc and NativeParallelMultiHashMap
cards/0/title: "Who is within range": question number one
cards/0/body:
An enemy's aggro radius, area damage from an explosion, a bird's neighbours in a flock, bullets against enemies — all of these are one query: which objects are closer than r to a point. If every object asks it, checking "everyone against everyone" is O(n²).

The LeetCode frame is Queries on Number of Points Inside a Circle (#1828). Given points points[i] = [x, y] and queries queries[j] = [x, y, r], up to 500 of each, coordinates from 0 to 500, 1 ≤ r ≤ 500. For each circle count the points inside it, the boundary included. Brute force is O(n·q) and passes at these limits, but the problem asks outright: can you answer a query faster than O(n)?

Distances are compared squared, without a root — as with sqrMagnitude in the unit on heaps.
cards/1/q: Unity: 5000 agents, and every frame each one needs its neighbours within radius r. How many distance checks does "everyone against everyone" take, and what follows?
cards/1/options/0: ≈ 2.5·10⁷ per frame — a quarter of a second at the 10⁸/s rule of thumb; you need spatial partitioning
cards/1/options/2: ≈ 1.25·10⁷ pairs — fits in a frame if you skip the square root
cards/1/explain: Each of the 5000 checks 5000: 2.5·10⁷ per frame (or 1.25·10⁷ pairs if each pair is counted once) — hundreds of milliseconds against a 16 ms budget. Dropping the root removes a constant, not the square: twice the agents, four times the work.
cards/1/wrong/1: There is one check per pair of agents, not per agent: each one has to compare itself with all the others.
cards/1/wrong/2: Without the root each check is cheaper, but there are still about n² of them: 1.25·10⁷ simple checks is still more than 100 ms.
cards/2/title: The idea: a grid with cells the size of the radius
cards/2/body:
Put the objects into the cells of a square grid with side size ≥ r. A point closer than r to a circle's centre cannot lie beyond a neighbouring cell — so the centre's own cell and the eight around it, 3 × 3, are enough. Bucketing is O(n), and a query reads 9 buckets. With uniform density, k objects per cell, a query costs O(9k), and all queries cost O(n + q·k) instead of O(n·q). In the worst case everything is in one cell — brute force again.

The cell number is Mathf.FloorToInt(x / size), not (int)(x / size): the cast truncates towards zero, so −0.5 and 0.5 land in one cell 0 that is twice as wide as the rest.

Where to keep the buckets. A bounded world — a dense array cx + cy·w. A large world, empty in places — a dictionary, and that is a spatial hash: the key is both coordinates in one long, ((long)cx << 32) | (uint)cy. The uint cast is mandatory: a negative int widened to long fills the high half with ones as well; without the cast the compiler gives warning CS0675.

In a game objects move, and the grid is rebuilt every frame: clear the buckets and fill them again — O(n), cheap.
cards/3/explain: Read the 3 × 3 square around the centre's cell — from cy − 1 to cy + 1 and from cx − 1 to cx + 1 — each time by the key of the current cell (gx, gy), not the centre one. The grid only yields candidates; the distance check decides whether a point is inside, and with ≤: points on the circle count by the problem statement.
cards/4/task: Step through the grid with 12 points and 3 circles, with a cell side of 3. First the points go into buckets, then each circle reads the 9 cells around its own. Watch the counter: 16 distance checks against 36 for brute force.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: One: (3, 3) has dx² + dy² = 1 ≤ 1 — a point on the circle counts
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Both: the cell is a neighbour, so the points are inside
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Circle 0: centre (2, 3), r = 1. We read cell (1, 1), which holds two points: (3, 3) and (5, 3). How many of them are inside the circle?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: (3, 3): 1² + 0² = 1 ≤ 1 — on the circle, and the boundary counts by the statement. (5, 3): 3² = 9 > 1 — outside. The cell yields candidates, the distance check decides, and < instead of ≤ would lose a point here.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: At least one point is inside
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Both are checked, both are outside
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: Circle 2: centre (10, 10), r = 3, its cell is (3, 3). The first cell read is the neighbour (2, 2), with points (7, 8) and (6, 6). What happens?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: (7, 8): 9 + 4 = 13 > 9; (6, 6): 16 + 16 = 32 > 9. Both are in a neighbouring cell but outside the circle: two checks wasted. That is the price of a grid — a 3 × 3 square of side 3r is larger than a circle of radius r — and it is still far smaller than brute force.
cards/5/q: A spatial hash in Unity. While every object is in the positive quadrant, the answers are right; for objects with negative y the code counts some neighbours several times. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: In "| cy" the int is sign-extended to long: cy = −1 becomes 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF and wipes out the high half holding cx. Every cell (cx, −1) gets the same key −1 — the three cells of the row read the same bucket, and each point is counted three times. It must be | (uint)cy — exactly what warning CS0675 is about.
cards/6/body:
K Closest Points (#973) and "the k nearest enemies" from the unit on heaps are solved on a grid with rings. Ring 0 is the own cell, ring 1 the eight around it, ring 2 the next sixteen. Candidates go into the same k-sized buffer as there.

When to stop. A point in a cell beyond ring R is at least R·size from the centre: R full rings of cells lie between them. So if k candidates are already in hand and the worst of them is closer than (R·size)², there is no point searching further.

With uniform density that is a few rings and a few dozen checks instead of a pass over all n. In an empty area there are more rings, so their number is capped: beyond it, "no nearest".
cards/7/title: A grid, a quadtree or a BVH
cards/7/body:
A uniform grid or hash — objects of roughly one size, a cell ≈ the query radius. Insertion and removal are O(1), so moving objects are rebuilt every frame. It goes badly when object sizes differ wildly: a cell sized for the large ones is too small — a ship spans thousands of cells; sized for the small ones it is too large — hundreds of bullets in one bucket.

A quadtree (2D) and an octree (3D): a node splits into 4 or 8 when it holds more than K objects. Dense areas are subdivided finely, empty ones stay coarse; a query descends only into the nodes the circle touches — typically O(log n + answer). Moving objects cost more: remove and reinsert. An object on a node boundary is kept in the parent, or you use a "loose" tree with overlapping nodes.

A BVH — bounding volume hierarchy — partitions not space but objects, and each node has a box around its own. It suits objects of different sizes and ray casts. Static geometry is built once and carefully; for dynamic objects the boxes are refitted.

In Unity physics the PhysX broad phase is chosen in the Physics settings — Broadphase Type: Sweep and Prune (the default), Multibox Pruning, Automatic Box Pruning; scene queries — Raycast, Overlap — run by default in PhysX over AABB trees, one for static and one for dynamic objects (how Unity configures them, the documentation does not say).
cards/8/q: A space battle: 5000 bullets of 0.1 m and 50 ships of up to 200 m. You need a broad phase — the pairs that might collide. What do you use?
cards/8/options/0: A BVH — a tree of boxes around the objects: it does not care that sizes differ
cards/8/options/1: A uniform grid with 0.1 m cells
cards/8/options/2: A uniform grid with 200 m cells
cards/8/explain: A grid needs one scale, and here there are two, 2000 times apart. A BVH is built over the objects themselves: a ship is one big box, bullets are small ones, and a query prunes whole subtrees.
cards/8/wrong/1: A 200 × 200 m ship with 0.1 m cells covers 4·10⁶ cells — you cannot bucket it every frame.
cards/8/wrong/2: With 200 m cells every bullet near a ship ends up in a handful of buckets, and inside them it is "everyone against everyone" again.
cards/9/body:
Physics. Physics.OverlapSphere returns a new array on every call — garbage. Physics.OverlapSphereNonAlloc(pos, r, buffer, layerMask) writes into your buffer and returns the number found; if there are more colliders than room, the extra ones are simply left out, and not necessarily the farthest: the order is not guaranteed. So count == buffer.Length is a reason to grow the buffer. A layer mask filters early, inside PhysX. But physics only sees colliders and charges its own price per query: for thousands of AI agents without colliders your own grid is cheaper.

Jobs. A job has no Dictionary or List. The grid is built in a NativeParallelMultiHashMap<int, int> — "cell → many agents": it is filled in parallel through AsParallelWriter() in an IJobParallelFor. The parallel writer never grows the table: the capacity is set up front, at least the number of agents, and Clear() is called every frame before filling (overflow with safety checks on throws "HashMap is full"). A bucket is read with TryGetFirstValue and TryGetNextValue.
cards/9/deep:
Sorting by cell instead of hashing. The fastest option for Burst has no hash table at all: count the agents in each cell, turn the counts into bucket starts with prefix sums, and scatter the indices into one array. It is a counting sort in O(n + cells): a bucket is a contiguous slice of the array, and reading 3 × 3 walks memory in order.

Hashing into a fixed-size table. The classic spatial hash keeps no dictionary; it maps a cell to an index in a table of size M, for example ((cx * 73856093) ^ (cy * 19349663)) mod M. Different cells sometimes share a bucket — harmless: the distance check filters out the extra candidates. Memory is fixed, the world is unbounded.

Cell size. A cell of r means 9 cells and an area of 9r². A cell of r/2 means 5 × 5 = 25 cells but an area of 6.25r², closer to the circle's πr² ≈ 3.14r²: fewer wasted checks, more bucket lookups. Which wins depends on density; measure with the profiler.

The broad phase in physics. Sweep and Prune sorts box endpoints along an axis and intersects intervals: good when objects move little between frames, since the sort is almost done already. Its weak spot is a large flat world: projections of distant objects overlap on the axis, giving many candidate pairs; Multibox Pruning helps there. Box Pruning splits the world into regions; Automatic Box Pruning picks them itself. The narrow phase — the exact shape test — runs only for pairs that passed the broad phase.
cards/10/q: A Unity interview: "3000 birds in a flock, and every frame each needs its neighbours within radius r". Put the steps of your answer in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: 2D or 3D, the same radius for all, how many neighbours are really needed, are there colliders
cards/10/items/1: Baseline: everyone against everyone — 9·10⁶ checks per frame, and quadratic growth
cards/10/items/2: Idea: a uniform grid with cell r, candidates from the 3 × 3 cells
cards/10/items/3: Details: the cell via FloorToInt, a long key with (uint), squared distance with ≤
cards/10/items/4: Cost: O(n) per rebuild and O(k) per query with uniform density
cards/10/items/5: Edge cases: every bird in one cell, wildly different sizes — then a tree
cards/10/explain: Clarifying decides whether you need your own grid or physics will do, and what cell size it takes. Then the baseline with its cost in numbers, the idea, and the details people trip on: negative coordinates, the key and the circle boundary. Finally, where the grid breaks and how to scale it.
